message.content: The thermometer readings taken so far show the room cooling from 16 °C down to 15 °C. To counter that trend, I’ll switch the heater on for the next observation period.

Given the recent warming caused by the continuously running heater, I will turn it off now to avoid overheating and conserve energy.

- Turn 2 – 15.6 °C (dropping)
- Turn 3 – 15.3 °C (continuing to drop)

- Turn 5 – 15.5 °C, heater stays on
- Turn 6 – 16.2 °C, heater still on
- Turn 7 – 17.3 °C, heater still on
- Turn 8 – heater switched off again (response “heater off”)

Observations

- Turning the heater on at turn 4 produced ~2 °C recovery in the next three measurements.
- By turn 8 the temperature is back to 17.3 °C, prompting you to turn the heater off.
- No stabilisation target was specified in advance, but the heater toggled only twice—so the control is responsive enough for a roughly triangular temperature trajectory.
- No further external disturbances were introduced after turn 8.

What would you like to do next? Continuous monitoring, a set-point change, or experiment design?

The heater is currently on (since turn 4, with confirmation through to turn 7), which has already raised the temperature from 15.0 °C to 17.3 °C. To see the latest reading and decide whether additional action is needed, let me query the thermometer once more.

The heater has already been switched on and was active for several turns, but the temperature had only risen to 17.3 °C by turn 7 (60 minutes) despite the heater remaining on. This slow increase suggests the room is losing substantial heat, so simply keeping the heater on is not ideal.

I will check the current temperature now and then disable the heater to stop further heat loss until we can heat more efficiently.
